rows.H1 Statement: Congress has difficulty attracting talent
rows.H1 Description: Entry-level roles run on unpaid or barely paid internships that filter for students who can afford to work for free, and starting salaries lose out to lobbying firms, agencies, and the private sector before a candidate ever applies.
rows.H3 Statement: Congress is a competitive employer
rows.H3 Description: Competitive initial compensation with benefits and recruitment beyond the networks that currently supply Capitol Hill make public legislative service an attractive first job.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress underinvests in its people
rows.H1 Description: Onboarding, mentorship, and training vary office by office with no institutional floor, so a staffer's grasp of procedure, policy, and oversight depends on where they landed rather than any deliberate investment.
rows.H3 Statement: Congress deliberately builds its workforce's expertise
rows.H3 Description: Structured onboarding, mentorship, and institution-wide HR standards give every staffer the same baseline knowledge regardless of which office hires them.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress has difficulty retaining talent
rows.H1 Description: Staff leave for lobbyists and agencies as their expertise matures, shifting the knowledge advantage to the very interests Congress is meant to scrutinize. A legislature that cannot think independently cannot govern independently.
rows.H3 Statement: Congress retains institutional knowledge
rows.H3 Description: Competitive pay, benefits, and career paths that let people build a life on the Hill turn a two-year stop into a career, keeping expertise in-house and preserving Congress's ability to execute effectively.

rows.H1 Statement: Interfaces between offices and support agencies are opaque
rows.H1 Description: Congressional offices and committees primarily submit requests to support agencies by email, leaving the requester with no visibility into status, timeline, or point of contact, and leaving the agency unable to easily aggregate volume and turnaround data it needs to assess its own performance.
rows.H3 Statement: Interfaces between offices and support agencies are transparent and easy to navigate
rows.H3 Description: Every request lives in a shared ticket tracking system where both sides can see its owner, status, and timeline, and where the accumulated record automatically gives agencies and their committees of jurisdiction aggregate performance data.

rows.H1 Statement: Support agencies cannot meet the demands of members and staff
rows.H1 Description: Requests to CRS, GAO, and Legislative Counsel arrive faster than they can be filled, and requesters have little visibility into how work is prioritized or where their request sits. Products often land long after the decision they were meant to inform.
rows.H3 Statement: Institutional knowledge is queryable on demand
rows.H3 Description: Support agency analysis is held in structured, queryable form that a staffer can search from a phone, so routine questions resolve immediately and analysts spend their time on work only they can do. Intake screening routes the rest to the right agency at the right depth.

rows.H1 Statement: Election incentives reward position-taking over legislating
rows.H1 Description: Primaries, district maps, and party fundraising expectations decide most races long before a general election, so the behavior that wins a seat has little to do with the work of governing once in it. Members arrive with no electoral reason to invest in the institution.
rows.H3 Statement: The path to reelection runs through governing
rows.H3 Description: District maps, primary structures, and campaign finance rules are set so that a member's standing with voters depends on what they legislate and deliver. Competing for the general election voter becomes the normal way to hold a seat.

rows.H1 Statement: Fundraising crowds out the legislative work of members
rows.H1 Description: Members spend a large share of the working day raising money, including party dues assessed on top of their own campaigns, with call time scheduled around votes and hearings rather than the reverse. Deliberation, oversight, and committee work are what is left over.
rows.H3 Statement: Members' time is spent legislating rather than raising money
rows.H3 Description: Campaign finance rules and party expectations no longer require perpetual fundraising, and the hours now spent on call time return to committee work, constituent engagement, and deliberation.

rows.H1 Statement: Public input into Congress is low quality
rows.H1 Description: Participation mostly diffuses tension rather than informing lawmaking. Offices lack the capacity to process input at scale, and deep distrust of representation means what does arrive rarely carries usable signal.
rows.H3 Statement: Public input is structured signal that shapes legislation
rows.H3 Description: Deliberation at scale produces clear, weighted signal about what constituents want and which tradeoffs they will accept. Commitments made in public are tracked over time, and a member can see how input moved a bill.

rows.H1 Statement: Constituent management systems are outdated and hold offices' data captive
rows.H1 Description: Offices run casework and constituent mail on a handful of approved vendor systems that store the office's history in proprietary formats, so changing tools means losing that history. Answering a question across offices means asking each one by hand.
rows.H3 Statement: Offices own their constituent data and choose the tools that sit on top of it
rows.H3 Description: Constituent records live in a shared, standards-based layer the institution owns, with vendors competing on the functions built above it. An office can switch tools, or aggregate across offices, without losing what it knows.

rows.H1 Statement: Congressional offices do not track stakeholder engagement
rows.H1 Description: Meetings with advocates, industry, and local organizations live in individual staffers' notes and calendars, so an office's knowledge of who wants what leaves when that staffer does. Offices cannot easily see who in the district a pending bill would affect.
rows.H3 Statement: Offices hold a durable record of who they hear from and what is at stake in the district
rows.H3 Description: Stakeholder contact and district impact are captured as structured data tied to bills and issues, so any staffer can see the history behind a position and members know who a vote reaches at home before they cast it.

rows.H1 Statement: There is no unified system for making funding requests to offices
rows.H1 Description: The House and Senate run separate request processes with separate forms and separate vetting, so committees spend the front of every cycle matching requests submitted to multiple offices to avoid funding the same project twice. Nothing routes a request to GAO or OMB before markup.
rows.H3 Statement: One pipeline carries a funding request from member to committee to oversight
rows.H3 Description: Every request enters through a single portal in a common format, is checked automatically for duplication, eligibility, and conflicts across both chambers and the executive branch, and carries that record forward, so oversight begins at the request rather than years after the money is spent.

rows.H1 Statement: Caseworkers are increasingly overloaded with requests
rows.H1 Description: Casework volume has grown many times over as constituents turn to Congress to reach agencies that have become slower or harder to reach, and much of what arrives is a request for publicly available information. Offices work hundreds of near-identical cases by hand in systems that cannot see each other.
rows.H3 Statement: Constituents' issues are addressed quickly and transparently
rows.H3 Description: Routine inquiries are triaged and answered at the front door, patterns across offices are visible in aggregate, and constituents can check the status of their own case without calling to ask. Caseworkers spend their time on the cases that need a human advocate.

rows.H1 Statement: Members are not incentivized to care about institutional power
rows.H1 Description: A member's standing depends on their party and the White House rather than on the strength of the branch they serve in, so ceding authority to the executive and failing to invest in the institution are considered politically safest.
rows.H3 Statement: Members have reason to defend the power of their own branch
rows.H3 Description: Congress exercises its authority routinely enough that giving it away is visible and costly, and members build careers on what they can accomplish through the institution rather than on their proximity to the executive.

rows.H1 Statement: Members are not incentivized to care about effective policymaking
rows.H1 Description: Most substantive policy moves on a few must-pass vehicles, so the rest of legislating is partisan position-taking, and the years between enactment and implementation mean credit rarely returns to whoever wrote the law. Nothing in the job rewards finding out whether a policy worked.
rows.H3 Statement: Legislating is rewarded on whether it works
rows.H3 Description: More bills move on their own rather than riding a single annual vehicle, results come back to the members who wrote them, and following a law into implementation is a normal part of the job rather than an optional interest.

rows.H1 Statement: Members' schedules are unpredictable and poorly used
rows.H1 Description: The annual calendar is set late and changes often, and committees schedule against each other with no binding way to deconflict, so members move between competing obligations rather than working through any of them. Planning a legislative strategy, or a life, around it is difficult.
rows.H3 Statement: Members' time is scheduled deliberately and predictably
rows.H3 Description: A stable calendar published well in advance, with block scheduling and enforced committee deconfliction, lets members be in one place doing one thing at a time and lets staff build legislative work around a known rhythm.

rows.H1 Statement: Floor time is shrinking and poorly used
rows.H1 Description: The chambers hold fewer legislative days than a generation ago, and much of that floor time goes to suspension bills and messaging votes whose outcomes are settled in advance, while real amendments and negotiation happen in leadership offices.
rows.H3 Statement: The floor is where legislation is debated, amended, and decided
rows.H3 Description: More session days go to bills that can be amended and voted on in the open, with predictable paths to the floor that do not depend entirely on leadership discretion, so a bill's fate is settled by votes rather than by scheduling.

rows.H1 Statement: Tech approval and procurement pipelines are clogged and fragmented
rows.H1 Description: Offices wait months for tool approvals, no channel aggregates demand across offices, and the House and Senate run separate, inconsistent vendor processes, so every office starts the same review from zero.
rows.H3 Statement: Congress acquires technology once, for the whole institution, at the speed of need
rows.H3 Description: A single security review is binding on both chambers, aggregated demand from offices triggers funded procurement automatically, and low-risk tools reach staff in days rather than quarters.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress lacks permanent in-house tech policy expertise
rows.H1 Description: The expertise Congress relies on is either scaled for an earlier era or borrowed temporarily from outside through fellows, detailees, and philanthropy, leaving no standing technical capacity the institution itself owns.
rows.H3 Statement: Congress owns standing, nonpartisan technical expertise
rows.H3 Description: Permanent technology assessment capacity sits inside the legislative branch, with career paths and pay that make it a real job rather than a fellowship year, so committees can get fast, credible technical answers without borrowing them.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress has little shared data or analytical infrastructure
rows.H1 Description: Common publishing standards exist for bill text, but analysis is built one committee and one contract at a time with no durable plumbing underneath, so evidence rarely reaches lawmaking in usable form and nothing built for one office carries over to the next.
rows.H3 Statement: Shared legislative data infrastructure the whole institution builds on
rows.H3 Description: Common data standards and durable, owned plumbing connect committees, offices, and support agencies. Analysis built once is reusable everywhere, and new tools start from infrastructure instead of from scratch.

rows.H1 Statement: No dedicated digital service serves all of Congress
rows.H1 Description: The House has a small digital service, the Senate has no equivalent, and the two chambers run separate infrastructure, vendor reviews, and systems for the same functions. Delivery capacity depends on a handful of people, and what is built for one chamber cannot be reused in the other.
rows.H3 Statement: A permanent technical corps sits inside Congress
rows.H3 Description: Standing in-house technical expertise across offices and committees, with career paths, pay scales, and hiring authorities that make technical work a normal congressional career rather than a borrowed exception.

rows.H1 Statement: The Senate cannot act on measures that hold majority support
rows.H1 Description: Ending debate on legislation takes sixty votes, so the chamber legislates through a narrow reconciliation path or not at all, and bills with broad bipartisan cosponsorship never receive a vote. Objecting costs a senator nothing and requires nothing on the record.
rows.H3 Statement: The Senate can act on measures that hold majority support
rows.H3 Description: Debate rules require senators to hold the floor to block a bill rather than to signal an objection, making obstruction visible and costly, so legislation with real support gets a vote instead of dying in the queue.

rows.H1 Statement: District offices are underserved by congressional infrastructure
rows.H1 Description: District staff carry most casework and constituent contact but sit at the end of systems, training, and support designed around Washington offices. What they learn about how policy is landing rarely reaches legislative staff.
rows.H3 Statement: District offices are fully supported members of the congressional workforce
rows.H3 Description: District staff get the same tools, training, and support as Washington staff, and what they hear from constituents feeds directly into the office's legislative and oversight work.

rows.H1 Statement: Committees are steadily losing power to leadership
rows.H1 Description: Agenda-setting, bill text, and negotiation have moved into leadership offices, leaving committees to hold hearings on bills they will not write. Chairs and their staff hold the subject matter expertise but decreasing control over what reaches the floor.
rows.H3 Statement: Committees are where legislation is written and negotiated
rows.H3 Description: Committees control their own agendas, are staffed and resourced to do the work, and report bills that leadership schedules rather than rewrites, making subject matter expertise the basis of legislative power again.

rows.H1 Statement: Pervasive risk aversion blocks experimentation
rows.H1 Description: The default institutional answer is no. Staff are penalized for trying new tools, first movers absorb the social and political risk, and innovation work sits under five or six layers of approval, so a small change takes months instead of weeks.
rows.H3 Statement: Experimentation is a normal, protected part of how the institution works
rows.H3 Description: Trying a new tool is unremarkable. Staff have standing authority to test low-risk technology, failure is treated as information rather than liability, and the path from a working prototype to something every office can use is measured in weeks.

rows.H1 Statement: Bill drafting and the US Code pipeline are archaic and opaque
rows.H1 Description: Staff cannot easily see how bill text modifies the US Code. The handoff among Legislative Counsel, the floor, and GPO is manual and error-prone, and no version control sits under the statute the process produces.
rows.H3 Statement: Statute is drafted, reviewed, and maintained under version control
rows.H3 Description: Drafters see a live diff of how a bill changes the US Code, the chain of custody from draft to enacted law is automated and auditable, and any staffer can trace a provision's history in seconds.

rows.H1 Statement: Government is funded by crisis rather than by process
rows.H1 Description: Appropriations bills almost never pass on time, so agencies run on continuing resolutions that carry forward last year's decisions, and the threat of a lapse becomes the negotiating instrument. What should be twelve deliberate decisions arrives as a year-end package or a full-year CR written under deadline.
rows.H3 Statement: Government is funded on time, every year
rows.H3 Description: The twelve bills move on a schedule the chambers can actually hold, with deadlines enforced by process rather than by shutdown risk, so agencies plan against real budgets and Congress makes funding choices deliberately.

rows.H1 Statement: Funding cannot be traced from what Congress approved to what was actually spent
rows.H1 Description: Committee reports, allocation tables, and project lists are published as PDFs and screenshots rather than data, and the House, Senate, and CBO run separate systems whose numbers must be reconciled by hand at every stage. Once money is enacted, connecting it to actual spending is manual work in an entirely different set of systems.
rows.H3 Statement: Machine readable appropriations data traceable from source to output
rows.H3 Description: Appropriations move as structured data through one shared system used across both chambers and CBO and published openly, so a dollar can be followed from request to enacted line to outlay without anyone rekeying a number.

rows.H1 Statement: The confirmation process crowds out the Senate's legislative work
rows.H1 Description: An administration opens with well over a thousand positions requiring Senate action. Batch consideration now clears sub-Cabinet nominees faster, but it concentrates the decision in the majority leader's hands, and the Senate still spends floor time on nominations that could go to legislating.
rows.H3 Statement: The Senate's confirmation attention goes to the positions that warrant it
rows.H3 Description: Routine positions clear through expedited processes and individual consideration is reserved for senior and lifetime appointments, so agencies are led by confirmed officials early and floor time returns to legislating.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress learns what agencies did long after they did it
rows.H1 Description: Oversight runs on hearings and document requests that arrive well after decisions are made, while the executive branch holds better data, faster procurement, and more technical capacity than the committees reviewing it. Routine staff-level contact between committees and agencies is thin, and formal channels default to no.
rows.H3 Statement: Feedback from implementation reaches Congress continuously
rows.H3 Description: Committees receive structured, ongoing information from agency implementation rather than episodic document dumps, with working staff-level channels and shared data that let Congress see problems as they develop and act while it still matters.

rows.H1 Statement: Congress has limited mechanisms to understand specific policy impacts on constituents
rows.H1 Description: No standing function tracks implementation, maps how a regulatory regime actually operates, or feeds what is learned back into legislating, so oversight lags the systems it governs by years.
rows.H3 Statement: Continuous “is this law working?” loops
rows.H3 Description: Learning whether a law works is a standing function of the branch. Implementation is tracked as a matter of course, findings return to the committees that wrote the law, and Congress can adapt statute continuously without institutional crisis.

rows.H1 Statement: Much of the public record of Congress is difficult to use
rows.H1 Description: Bill text and roll call votes are well structured and available through Congress.gov, but hearings, committee reports, amendments, and supporting documents are scattered across separate systems as PDFs and scanned images, most without an API. Whether a record is usable depends on which part of the institution produced it.
rows.H3 Statement: Congressional records and documents are easily accessible to the public
rows.H3 Description: Everything Congress produces is published as structured data through a common interface as soon as it exists, searchable across both chambers and across years by researchers, journalists, staff, and AI agents.

rows.H1 Statement: Committee jurisdictions are outdated and misaligned across chambers and agencies
rows.H1 Description: House jurisdictions run on Rule X plus a layer of precedent and inter-committee agreements, last comprehensively realigned in the 1970s with a narrower round of changes in 1995. The Senate's Rule XXV map was drawn separately and does not parallel it. Issues that cut across agencies, from homeland security to artificial intelligence, are split among panels that match neither each other nor the executive branch they oversee, so a cross-agency bill needs multiple referrals in each chamber and faces a different set of committees on each side of the Capitol.
rows.H3 Statement: Jurisdictions match the problems Congress legislates on
rows.H3 Description: Committee jurisdictions are drawn around how government actually works and reviewed on a set cadence rather than left to accumulate through precedent. The two chambers' maps correspond closely enough that a bill meets a comparable set of committees in each, and a measure spanning several agencies has one committee accountable for it rather than five with partial claims.

An administration opens with well over a thousand positions requiring Senate action. Batch consideration now clears sub-Cabinet nominees faster, but it concentrates the decision in the majority leader's hands, and the Senate still spends floor time on nominations that could go to legislating.
The Senate's confirmation attention goes to the positions that warrant it

Routine positions clear through expedited processes and individual consideration is reserved for senior and lifetime appointments, so agencies are led by confirmed officials early and floor time returns to legislating.
Oversight
Oversight
Congress learns what agencies did long after they did it

Oversight runs on hearings and document requests that arrive well after decisions are made, while the executive branch holds better data, faster procurement, and more technical capacity than the committees reviewing it. Routine staff-level contact between committees and agencies is thin, and formal channels default to no.
Feedback from implementation reaches Congress continuously

Committees receive structured, ongoing information from agency implementation rather than episodic document dumps, with working staff-level channels and shared data that let Congress see problems as they develop and act while it still matters.
Institutional Capacity, Oversight
Constituent Engagement
Congress has limited mechanisms to understand specific policy impacts on constituents
No standing function tracks implementation, maps how a regulatory regime actually operates, or feeds what is learned back into legislating, so oversight lags the systems it governs by years.
Continuous “is this law working?” loops

Learning whether a law works is a standing function of the branch. Implementation is tracked as a matter of course, findings return to the committees that wrote the law, and Congress can adapt statute continuously without institutional crisis.
Technology & Systems, Information
Legislation, House, Senate
Much of the public record of Congress is difficult to use

Bill text and roll call votes are well structured and available through Congress.gov, but hearings, committee reports, amendments, and supporting documents are scattered across separate systems as PDFs and scanned images, most without an API. Whether a record is usable depends on which part of the institution produced it.
Congressional records and documents are easily accessible to the public

Everything Congress produces is published as structured data through a common interface as soon as it exists, searchable across both chambers and across years by researchers, journalists, staff, and AI agents.
Institutional Capacity
Committees, Structure, Oversight
Committee jurisdictions are outdated and misaligned across chambers and agencies

House jurisdictions run on Rule X plus a layer of precedent and inter-committee agreements, last comprehensively realigned in the 1970s with a narrower round of changes in 1995. The Senate's Rule XXV map was drawn separately and does not parallel it. Issues that cut across agencies, from homeland security to artificial intelligence, are split among panels that match neither each other nor the executive branch they oversee, so a cross-agency bill needs multiple referrals in each chamber and faces a different set of committees on each side of the Capitol.
Jurisdictions match the problems Congress legislates on

Committee jurisdictions are drawn around how government actually works and reviewed on a set cadence rather than left to accumulate through precedent. The two chambers' maps correspond closely enough that a bill meets a comparable set of committees in each, and a measure spanning several agencies has one committee accountable for it rather than five with partial claims.

rows.Problem Statement: Senate interns and intern coordinators are unsupported
rows.Problem Description: The House Intern Resource Office (HIRO), created on a Select Committee on Modernization recommendation, centralizes House internships: onboarding, professional development, coordinator training, and institution-wide data collection. The Senate has none, so each office builds its own; quality depends on where an intern lands, and the chamber cannot count unpaid interns or report demographics beyond what payroll disclosures incidentally capture.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Senate Intern Resource Office
rows.Solution Description: Fund a Senate counterpart to HIRO: consistent onboarding and professional development for interns and the staffers who manage them, plus records on intern numbers, pay, and demographics, now left to outside organizations. Voluntary use preserves each Senator's authority while sparing offices a start from scratch. Keep it Senate-specific rather than a HIRO extension, since the chambers run on different rules and traditions.
rows.Horizon Justification: Interns are the Senate's main talent pipeline; a standing office strengthens it at the entry point.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Senate Sergeant at Arms Karen Gibson asked the Legislative Branch Appropriations subcommittee for two FTEs in FY2025; no funding has been dedicated.

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional pay is set office by office with no underlying structure
rows.Problem Description: Each office sets salaries from its own allowance, so pay for the same job varies widely, there is no automatic adjustment for inflation, and a raise depends on a staffer's chief of staff rather than on a schedule. Junior salaries lose to agencies and firms, and mid-career staff leave before their expertise matures.
rows.Solution Statement: Put congressional staff on a structured pay scale
rows.Solution Description: Move staff onto a GS-style scale with defined bands by role and seniority and automatic cost-of-living adjustments, raising junior salaries meaningfully while leaving offices discretion within each band, so pay becomes a property of the job rather than a negotiation each staffer runs alone. Proposals converge on the scale but differ on mechanism: apply the GS scale to committee staff or to all staff; make the existing link between the House staff pay cap and Executive Schedule Level II automatic rather than requiring a fresh Speaker's Pay Order each Congress; raise or remove the personal office staff cap, unchanged since the late 1970s while average district population rose from 519,235 to 761,169; and direct the CAO to build an inflation-indexing mechanism applied annually to the office allowance formula.
rows.Horizon Justification: Automatic adjustment removes the annual political decision that keeps pay flat, so the fix persists through changes in leadership and budget climate rather than eroding between one-time increases.
rows.Current Status (Optional): House set a $45,000 minimum staff salary in 2022; no scale exists in either chamber

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional pay is set office by office with no underlying structure
rows.Problem Description: Offices cannot raise salaries beyond what their allowance supports, and the allowance has not tracked the cost of running an office or of living in Washington.
rows.Solution Statement: One-time increases to the members representational allowance
rows.Solution Description: Raise the MRA and staff pay caps in a single appropriations cycle so offices can pay more immediately, as the House did during the Select Committee period. The House Inspector General sized the shortfall at roughly $42,000 more per office, about $333 million House-wide, for pay parity alone, and the FY2022 committee funding increase of 21 percent only restored 2010-era levels. Offices are legally permitted 22 staff but funded for 16 or 17, and only five or six reach the authorized limit.
rows.Horizon Justification: The increase is real but decays. Without indexing, the same fight has to be won every few years, and nothing changes how pay is set inside offices.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #2. The recurring fight to win one-time MRA increases generates the shortfall data and political pressure that make the case for replacing the manual increase with an automatic, indexed pay scale, so the fix no longer has to be won every cycle.
rows.Current Status (Optional): A one-time 21% MRA increase was enacted during the Select Committee period

rows.Problem Statement: Congress borrows technical expertise instead of owning it
rows.Problem Description: Technologists reach the Hill through philanthropy-funded fellowships and agency details, typically for a year, of which perhaps half is productive once onboarding and clearance are done. The person leaves with what they learned.
rows.Solution Statement: Technology fellowships and agency detailees
rows.Solution Description: Continue placing fellows and detailees in offices and committees to fill immediate technical gaps, with the fellow choosing their placement and the host office bearing no salary cost, and build a conversion path on top of that: extend the Intern Resource Office's mandate to cover fellows, create a fellow registry using a bona fide agreement as the registration instrument on the model of Senate Rule 41, give departing fellows access to internal job postings and the resume bank, give hiring offices conversion guidance covering budget and slot timing, and report annual conversion rates as the primary metric. The benchmark to beat is roughly 130 technologists placed over a decade, of whom 30 converted to long-term staff.
rows.Horizon Justification: Each placement helps one office and quietly reduces the pressure to fund permanent technical staff, so the institution stays dependent on outside money for a capability it should own.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #121. The fellowship program's conversion tracking, hiring guidance, and job-posting access build a demonstrated pipeline of technologists willing to work on the Hill, giving committees the recruiting evidence and workflow needed to justify permanent, committee-housed technical positions.
rows.Current Status (Optional): TechCongress and agency details operate today; no conversion path to permanent roles

rows.Problem Statement: Staff development depends on which office hires you
rows.Problem Description: Institution-wide training exists but participation is optional and uneven, so onboarding, mentorship, and procedural knowledge vary sharply across offices and committees.
rows.Solution Statement: Institution-wide onboarding and professional development standards
rows.Solution Description: Establish a baseline curriculum every new staffer completes, structured mentorship across offices, and HR standards that apply chamber-wide, delivered through the existing staff academies and expanded to the Senate. Two proposals arrive at this independently, both framing better onboarding and ongoing training as a precondition for member and staff effectiveness rather than as a benefit.
rows.Horizon Justification: Making a floor institutional rather than optional changes what every staffer knows regardless of where they land, and the standard survives the turnover of any particular chief of staff.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Congressional Staff Academy exists in the House; participation is discretionary

rows.Problem Statement: Staff development depends on which office hires you
rows.Problem Description: Outside organizations design and pay for much of the training that reaches staff, and it reaches only the staffers whose offices let them attend.
rows.Solution Statement: Outside-funded training programs and peer networks
rows.Solution Description: Philanthropy and civil society run cohort programs, peer networks, and skills training that lift staff capability across many offices at once.
rows.Horizon Justification: It demonstrates what good training looks like while supplying it from outside, which reduces the pressure on Congress to fund the same thing permanently.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #5. Outside-funded cohort programs and peer networks demonstrate what good training looks like and which content works, giving the institution a tested curriculum and format to adopt as a required, chamber-wide onboarding and development standard.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Multiple programs operate today across both chambers

rows.Problem Statement: Congress has no standing nonpartisan technical assessment capacity
rows.Problem Description: The Office of Technology Assessment, which produced independent technology assessments for Congress, was defunded in 1995, and nothing has replaced its function of giving committees credible technical analysis they did not have to borrow.
rows.Solution Statement: Reestablish an Office of Technology Assessment
rows.Solution Description: Fund a permanent nonpartisan technology assessment office serving both chambers, designed for faster turnaround than the original, with authority to convene outside expertise and report directly to committees. Proposals disagree on where the function should sit: one locates science and technology assessment in a new House office under House Administration, carried in row 86; another places it as a hub inside GAO connecting members and staff to outside experts.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a standing institutional capability rather than a temporary one, and the absence of that capability is what keeps regenerating the problem across every new technology cycle.
rows.Current Status (Optional): OTA remains authorized but unfunded; reestablishment bills have been introduced repeatedly since 2018

rows.Additional Tags: organization, coordination, in house development, CAO
rows.Problem Statement: No office owns congressional capacity and technology as its job
rows.Problem Description: Modernization work is spread across the CAO, the Sergeants at Arms, the Library, GPO, and committee staff, with no entity responsible for the institution's overall capacity and no one whose job it is to think past the current Congress.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Congressional Capacity and Technology Office
rows.Solution Description: Create a single office responsible for legislative branch capacity and technology across both chambers, combining technology assessment, delivery support, and institutional strategy, with its own appropriation and a defined relationship to House Administration and Senate Rules.
rows.Horizon Justification: It gives modernization a permanent owner with budget and standing, which the current arrangement lacks, and consolidates functions now split by chamber.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by POPVOX Foundation; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Congress has no standing nonpartisan technical assessment capacity
rows.Problem Description: Standing up a permanent office requires appropriations and hiring authority that take years, while committees need technical answers now.
rows.Solution Statement: Shadow technology assessment office staffed by academic rotators
rows.Solution Description: Run a two-year trial staffed by university researchers on short rotations, modeled on the NSF rotator program and the UK Parliament's POST, delivering quick-turnaround briefings and direct technical assistance without permanent hiring. Following the UK routing model, committees certify questions, the office sends them to academics trained to answer in short fact-grounded form, and the office reviews and forwards the responses. Estimated cost is under $1 million annually, and the Clerk has to be engaged on submissions for the record.
rows.Horizon Justification: A rotating trial supplies briefings without building anything the institution keeps, and its two-year horizon means the expertise leaves at exactly the point it becomes most useful.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #7. The rotator-staffed shadow office tests the routing model (committee certifies a question, an assessor answers, the office reviews) and shows the cost and demand at low risk, providing the working template a permanent OTA can scale up.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Concept stage

rows.Additional Tags: in house development, organization, coordination, CAO
rows.Problem Statement: The Senate has no digital service
rows.Problem Description: The House has a small digital service inside the CAO. The Senate has no equivalent, so Senate offices and committees have nowhere to go for internal product development, and nothing built in the House has a counterpart to adopt it.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Senate digital service
rows.Solution Description: Fund a delivery team inside the Senate with product, design, and engineering staff, working on constituent systems, committee tools, and floor operations, and structured from the start to coordinate with its House counterpart.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates permanent delivery capacity in the chamber that has none, and gives bicameral work an actual counterparty rather than one chamber trying to build for both.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Raised by Senate and House staff in interviews; not funded

rows.Additional Tags: coordination, organization, in house development, procurement
rows.Problem Statement: Congress runs duplicate technology infrastructure by chamber
rows.Problem Description: The House and Senate maintain separate infrastructure, separate vendor processes, and separate systems for identical functions, and the Architect of the Capitol, Library, and GPO sit outside both. Nothing built once is reused.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Congress-wide digital service with integrated bicameral infrastructure
rows.Solution Description: Evolve the House Digital Service and a new Senate counterpart into a single congressional digital service, and integrate the underlying IT infrastructure across the House, Senate, AOC, Library, GPO, and committees under joint governance.
rows.Horizon Justification: Merging delivery capacity and infrastructure into one governed institution changes the structure that regenerates duplication, rather than making the duplicated processes individually faster.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Championed by multiple interviewees; House Digital Service exists in one chamber only

rows.Problem Statement: No committee owns technology across the institution
rows.Problem Description: House Administration and Senate Rules each handle their own chamber, so decisions about shared infrastructure have no common forum and no single committee can commit both chambers to a standard.
rows.Solution Statement: Joint committee on technology
rows.Solution Description: Create a joint committee with jurisdiction over legislative branch technology and data standards, able to authorize shared infrastructure and bind both chambers to common requirements. The competing structure is a standing technology committee in each chamber rather than a joint one, on the grounds that many committees hold technology hearings today and none owns the subject.
rows.Horizon Justification: A joint venue makes bicameral decisions possible at all, which is the precondition for every shared system proposed elsewhere in this list.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by CMF and others; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Tool approval takes months and every office starts from zero
rows.Problem Description: Offices wait months for approvals, vendors build against long requirement lists before they can demo, and no channel aggregates demand, so the same review runs office by office.
rows.Solution Statement: Fast-track review lanes and a demand aggregation portal
rows.Solution Description: Create expedited review for low-risk tools, a portal where offices request and upvote workflows so demand is visible, and pre-negotiated security reviews that can be reused. Hold the review itself to a standard: give vendors in cybersecurity review a substantive status update at least every 30 days naming outstanding requirements and next steps, require a monthly report to House Administration on the status, age, and disposition of every product in the pipeline in a consistent format, and publish review criteria and expected timeline at intake.
rows.Horizon Justification: Faster lanes shorten waits inside the existing structure, but bicameral duplication and the absence of an institution-wide owner survive intact, so approvals still reset office by office.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #14. The fast-track lanes and demand portal expose how much of the review burden is duplicated across offices and chambers, building the evidence and the reusable pre-negotiated reviews that support merging both chambers into one binding security review.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Recognized problem; no unified process exists

rows.Problem Statement: Tool approval takes months and every office starts from zero
rows.Problem Description: A vendor approved in one chamber must start over in the other, and a security review completed once counts only where it was done.
rows.Solution Statement: One security review binding on both chambers
rows.Solution Description: Establish a single legislative branch security and privacy review whose outcome binds the House and Senate, with a shared approved-vendor list and a published requirements set that is pruned on a schedule.
rows.Horizon Justification: It eliminates the duplication at its source rather than accelerating each duplicate process, and turns approvals into an asset the institution accumulates.
rows.Current Status (Optional): No shared review exists; chambers maintain separate lists

rows.Problem Statement: Staff cannot experiment with new tools without personal risk
rows.Problem Description: Trying an unapproved tool exposes a staffer to political and professional risk, so experimentation happens quietly or not at all, and training cannot be offered on tools staff already use informally.
rows.Solution Statement: Sanctioned coding and AI sandboxes for staff
rows.Solution Description: Stand up pre-approved environments where staff can test AI and development tools against non-sensitive data without procurement or political exposure, paired with training. The standing version is an AI Center of Excellence with dedicated staff, member services, and a sandbox environment, described as achievable in the current appropriations cycle without waiting for a broader capacity review.
rows.Horizon Justification: A sandbox gives a few staffers room to try things while the approval layers and default no that produced the problem remain fully in place.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #16. The sandbox generates a track record of staff testing tools without incident, giving a named office the evidence needed to justify delegating standing authority to approve low-risk technology within days rather than requiring a sandbox workaround for every trial.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Not approved today; a GAO test kitchen existed but its outputs never reached the Hill

rows.Problem Statement: Staff cannot experiment with new tools without personal risk
rows.Problem Description: Innovation work sits under five or six layers of approval, so a small change takes months, and the institutional default answer to anything new is no.
rows.Solution Statement: Standing authority to approve low-risk technology
rows.Solution Description: Delegate authority to a named office to approve low-risk tools within days under published criteria, publish each decision and its reasoning, and treat a failed pilot as information rather than liability.
rows.Horizon Justification: Changing who can say yes, and how fast, addresses the condition that produces risk aversion rather than routing individual staff around it.
rows.Current Status (Optional): No such delegated authority exists

rows.Additional Tags: GAO, in house development, organization, norms
rows.Problem Statement: Innovation dies inside support agencies before it reaches Congress
rows.Problem Description: Prototypes built inside support agencies are constrained by host-agency risk culture and rarely reach members or staff, so capability exists that the institution never sees.
rows.Solution Statement: Independent innovation unit for the legislative branch
rows.Solution Description: Create a unit with DARPA-style independence from host-agency risk culture, its own budget, and a mandate to ship working demos to members and staff, killing and starting projects quickly.
rows.Horizon Justification: Structural independence changes the condition that kills the work rather than routing around it, and a standing mandate creates capability that survives any individual champion.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Concept only; GAO's STAA exists but is constrained by host agency culture

rows.Problem Statement: Prototypes rarely reach production
rows.Problem Description: Delivery capacity sits outside the institution or inside one-off events, and demos built by outside participants have no owner, no maintenance line, and no route into the systems staff use.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional Hackathon
rows.Solution Description: Convene staff, civil society, and technologists to build prototypes against real congressional problems, showcasing what modern tools could do.
rows.Horizon Justification: It proves the possible and builds relationships, but risks being read as evidence the problem is being handled rather than that it is structural.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #103. A hackathon produces working prototypes and relationships with outside technologists but no office empowered to adopt or maintain them; refounding the House Digital Service as an independent office with its own hiring authority gives those demos an owner that can carry them into production.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Held periodically since 2011

rows.Problem Statement: Requests to support agencies disappear into email
rows.Problem Description: Offices and committees submit most requests by email, so requesters cannot see status, owner, or timeline, and agencies cannot aggregate the volume and turnaround data needed to assess their own performance.
rows.Solution Statement: Shared request tracking system across support agencies
rows.Solution Description: Put every congressional request into a shared ticketing system visible to both sides, showing owner, status, and expected timeline; the accumulated record produces aggregate performance data for the agencies and their committees of jurisdiction.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes the interface between Congress and its agencies permanently and generates the performance data that oversight of those agencies lacks.
rows.Current Status (Optional): No shared system exists

rows.Problem Statement: Support agencies cannot meet demand and cannot explain how they triage
rows.Problem Description: Legislative Counsel, CRS, and GAO are all described as overwhelmed, with prioritization invisible to requesters, so seniority and persistence determine who gets served.
rows.Solution Statement: Request prescreening, triage guidance, and user feedback
rows.Solution Description: Publish screening questions requesters answer before submitting, route requests by type and depth, and let users rate reports and analysts so quality signal reaches the agency.
rows.Horizon Justification: Better triage rations a fixed supply more fairly without adding capacity, so the queue remains and the underlying staffing shortfall is untouched.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #21. Publishing triage criteria and collecting user ratings on quality generates the turnaround and demand data that support tying support-agency funding to published capacity targets under multi-year appropriations, rather than rationing a fixed staff pool more fairly.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Concept stage; GAO publishes protocols but Leg Counsel and CRS do not

rows.Problem Statement: Support agencies cannot meet demand
rows.Problem Description: Request volume has risen while agency staffing has not, and annual funding cycles make it impossible to plan multi-year work or compete for technical hires.
rows.Solution Statement: Multi-year budgets and staffing for support agencies
rows.Solution Description: Fund CRS, GAO, CBO, and Legislative Counsel on multi-year appropriations with dedicated hiring authority, tied to published capacity and turnaround targets.
rows.Horizon Justification: Multi-year funding changes what the agencies can plan and hire for, which one-time increases cannot, and ties capacity to measurable commitments.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Requested repeatedly in legislative branch appropriations testimony

rows.Additional Tags: GAO, CRS, CBO, data transparency, in house development
rows.Problem Statement: Institutional knowledge is locked in formats staff cannot query
rows.Problem Description: Decades of GAO, CRS, and CBO analysis sit in PDFs, recommendations are not tracked to closure, and a staffer with a question at 9pm has no way to search what the institution already knows.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional intelligence platform over support agency content
rows.Solution Description: Convert support agency output into structured, retrieval-ready formats and expose a secure assistant that members and staff can query, including sensitive material under existing protocols, and open-source the internal tools the agencies already built.
rows.Horizon Justification: It turns expertise Congress has already paid for into a permanent, queryable asset the institution owns, changing how knowledge reaches staff rather than how much of it is produced.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Prototype-feasible; GAO has run internal retrieval experiments that never reached the Hill

rows.Problem Statement: Analysis is built one committee and one contract at a time
rows.Problem Description: Publishing standards exist for bill text but there is no shared analytical plumbing, so tools built for one committee cannot be reused, and evidence rarely reaches lawmaking in usable form.
rows.Solution Statement: Shared legislative data standards and infrastructure
rows.Solution Description: Establish common data standards and identifiers across committees, offices, and support agencies, with durable shared infrastructure owned by a support office and a maintenance line attached.
rows.Horizon Justification: Replacing per-committee one-offs with infrastructure the whole institution builds on changes what every future tool starts from.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Bulk Data Task Force exists as a coordinating body; no shared analytical infrastructure

rows.Problem Statement: Analysis is built one committee and one contract at a time
rows.Problem Description: A committee with a pressing analytical need contracts for a tool that meets it, built against that committee's data and workflow.
rows.Solution Statement: One-time committee analytics tool
rows.Solution Description: Deliver a bespoke analytical tool to a single committee for a single need, on that committee's timeline.
rows.Horizon Justification: It produces real insight now and relieves exactly the pressure that might otherwise have produced standing analytical infrastructure.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #23. Building one bespoke analytics tool for a single committee surfaces the data fields, identifiers, and workflow patterns that a shared data standard needs, giving the institution a concrete first case to generalize into durable cross-committee infrastructure.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Common practice today

rows.Problem Statement: Most of the congressional record is published but not usable
rows.Problem Description: Bill text and votes are well structured, but hearings, committee reports, amendments, and supporting documents are scattered across systems as PDFs and scanned images, with no API and no way to search across them.
rows.Solution Statement: Bulk data and APIs for the full congressional record
rows.Solution Description: Publish hearings, reports, amendments, and supporting documents as structured data through a common API on the same footing as bill text, with persistent identifiers linking documents to the measures they concern.
rows.Horizon Justification: It makes the institution's own record queryable by Congress and the public alike, and every downstream tool depends on this being true.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Partial; Congress.gov and GovInfo APIs cover some collections

rows.Problem Statement: Staff cannot see how a bill changes existing law
rows.Problem Description: Drafters and reviewers work from bill text and the US Code as separate documents, and the handoff among Legislative Counsel, the floor, and GPO is manual.
rows.Solution Statement: Bill-to-Code diff demo tool
rows.Solution Description: Build a lightweight tool showing how a bill written in English compiles into changes to the US Code, giving drafters and reviewers a live diff view, positioned as a demo to build appetite for deeper reform.
rows.Horizon Justification: A demo makes the pipeline legible to whoever sees it while the statutory chain of custody, the manual handoffs, and the absence of version control continue unchanged underneath.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #27. The bill-to-code demo, built explicitly to create appetite for deeper reform, shows staff what a live diff between bill text and the US Code looks like, making the case for putting the Code itself under version control with a consolidated drafting pipeline.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Not built; identified as a low-lift proof of concept

rows.Additional Tags: GPO, organization, in house development, operations
rows.Problem Statement: Statute is produced without version control
rows.Problem Description: No system tracks the chain of custody from draft to enacted law, changes are annotated by hand at conference, and the offices that draft, codify, and print statute are separate organizations with separate systems.
rows.Solution Statement: US Code under version control with consolidated drafting offices
rows.Solution Description: Run statute as a version-controlled repository with chamber branches merging at conference and enactment as the merge to main, and consolidate the drafting, codification, and printing offices into one organization owning the pipeline end to end.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes the artifact itself, not the tooling around it, so provenance and traceability become properties of the law rather than something reconstructed after the fact.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Concept stage

rows.Problem Statement: Appropriations decisions are published as pictures of tables
rows.Problem Description: Committee reports, allocation tables, and project lists are released as PDFs and screenshots rather than data, so tracking what was funded requires manual extraction and nobody can reconcile enacted amounts against spending without rekeying numbers.
rows.Solution Statement: Machine-readable appropriations data and API
rows.Solution Description: Publish committee tables, allocations, and project lists as structured data through an API from the moment they are released, with identifiers that link an enacted line to agency spending reporting.
rows.Horizon Justification: Publishing appropriations as data makes the whole funding lifecycle traceable and removes the manual step where errors and opacity are introduced.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Some front offices push for machine-readable tables; GPO releases screenshots of PDFs

rows.Problem Statement: The three institutions writing appropriations do not share a data system
rows.Problem Description: CBO and the two appropriations committees each run separate legacy tracking and scoring tools with no common data structure, so every movement between chambers or new score means days of manual reconciliation.
rows.Solution Statement: One shared appropriations data system
rows.Solution Description: Build a single system of record for appropriations text, amendments, allocations, and scores, used by the House, Senate, and CBO, updating in real time for all three.
rows.Horizon Justification: One system of record eliminates reconciliation as a category of work rather than speeding it up, and the friction it removes is worst exactly where negotiation happens.
rows.Current Status (Optional): No shared system; each body maintains its own

rows.Problem Statement: Conference reconciliation is done by hand
rows.Problem Description: Conferees review master side-by-sides, changes are annotated manually, and final read-throughs of a single bill can run eight hours, typically overnight.
rows.Solution Statement: Automate the conference side-by-side
rows.Solution Description: Replace manual side-by-sides with generated comparisons and automated change tracking so conferees review a reliable diff rather than reconciling documents by hand.
rows.Horizon Justification: It removes hours of mechanical work without changing the separate systems that make reconciliation necessary, and some staff value the exhaustion as a forcing function for setting priorities.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #29. Automating the conference side-by-side proves that generated, reliable diffs can replace manual reconciliation for a single bill, building the technical case and comparison logic for one shared system of record spanning the House, Senate, and CBO.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Manual today

rows.Problem Statement: Funding requests have no unified pipeline
rows.Problem Description: The House and Senate run separate request processes with separate forms and vetting. Committees spend the front of every cycle matching duplicate requests by hand, and nothing routes a request to GAO or OMB before markup.
rows.Solution Statement: Unified funding request portal with automated GAO and OMB checks
rows.Solution Description: Route every request through one portal in a common format, check automatically for duplication, eligibility, and conflicts of interest against both chambers and the executive branch, and carry that record forward into oversight. Two competing positions attach to this. One holds that member-directed spending should continue but under standardized centralized disclosure, replacing the inconsistent committee PDFs offices publish today. The other holds that the ban should be restored outright, on the argument that member-directed spending fixes nothing and adds spending.
rows.Horizon Justification: Oversight begins at the request rather than years after the money is spent, and duplicate detection becomes a property of the system instead of committee labor.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Chambers run separate processes; GAO reviews a sample of projects after enactment

rows.Problem Statement: Funding requests have no unified pipeline
rows.Problem Description: Committees receive the same project request through multiple member offices across both chambers with no shared identifier, creating a real risk of funding one project twice.
rows.Solution Statement: Duplicate matching tools for funding requests
rows.Solution Description: Use text matching to identify the same request submitted to multiple offices across chambers, flagging likely duplicates for committee review.
rows.Horizon Justification: It catches duplicates after they enter two separate pipelines, leaving the separate pipelines, separate forms, and absent oversight linkage as they are.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #31. Text-matching duplicate flags surface how often the same request travels through separate office pipelines with no shared identifier, building the case for routing every request through one portal with automated duplication and eligibility checks from intake.
rows.Current Status (Optional): In use by committee staff

rows.Additional Tags: rules, time management, committee, data transparency
rows.Problem Statement: Appropriations almost never pass on time
rows.Problem Description: Twelve bills have to clear both chambers annually, and the work compresses into a year-end package written under deadline or a continuing resolution that carries last year's numbers forward.
rows.Solution Statement: Biennial two-year appropriations cycle
rows.Solution Description: Move appropriations to a two-year cycle, with the off year reserved for authorization and oversight work, on the theory that halving the frequency makes the deadline achievable. The variant that has come closest pairs a biennial budget resolution with annual appropriations, the core mark of the 2018 Joint Select Committee on Budget and Appropriations Process Reform and of the Enzi-Whitehouse proposal, and restricts single-year appropriations bills in the first year of a biennium. The source catalog flags its own proposals as contradictory.
rows.Horizon Justification: Stretching the timeline gives requests more time to accumulate while parochial spending, committee turf, and election-year pressure stay as they are, and the off year gets absorbed by the same politics. It treats time pressure rather than the fragmented data, weak transparency, and incentives underneath it.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #125. A biennial cycle alone stretches the timeline without changing who sits in the room or how decisions sequence; folding it into the broader budget resolution redesign, with fixed deadlines and reordered committee roles, addresses the turf and incentive problems the biennial fix leaves standing.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed repeatedly since the 1980s; never enacted

rows.Problem Statement: Spending and authorization have come apart
rows.Problem Description: A large share of annual appropriations funds programs whose authorizations have expired, so the committees with subject matter expertise no longer gate the money, and no one asks whether a program worked before it is funded again.
rows.Solution Statement: Merge the appropriating and authorizing committees
rows.Solution Description: Combine appropriations and authorizing jurisdiction so the same committee that reviews whether a program works also decides whether it is funded, ending the practice of funding lapsed authorizations. The scale is documented: CBO identified 1,326 authorizations that expired before FY2025, with roughly $500 billion of FY2025 appropriations tied to 457 of them.
rows.Horizon Justification: It rejoins the two decisions that were split apart, the condition that produces unauthorized spending and the loss of program review, and it restores subject matter expertise to the funding decision.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Hundreds of billions annually flow to expired authorizations; proposal raised by multiple interviewees and strongly opposed by appropriators

rows.Problem Statement: Funding lapses are used as leverage
rows.Problem Description: The threat of a shutdown is the instrument that forces year-end deals, and agencies absorb the cost of planning against a deadline that may not hold. Agencies ran on continuing appropriations an average of 118 days a year from FY1998 to FY2025.
rows.Solution Statement: Automatic continuing resolution
rows.Solution Description: Provide that if appropriations lapse, funding continues automatically at the prior year's level, removing the shutdown as an event. The leading vehicle is a rolling 14-day continuing resolution that restricts member travel and bars other business until appropriations finish; a related incentive device holds member salaries in escrow when a chamber has not adopted a budget resolution. The objection is that an automatic CR transfers leverage to a determined minority, and that a President could veto appropriations to hold the automatic funding in place indefinitely.
rows.Horizon Justification: It removes the crisis while freezing last year's decisions indefinitely, and it can reduce the pressure that now forces any agreement at all.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #125. An automatic CR removes the shutdown threat that currently forces last-minute deals, taking hostage-taking off the table so the underlying budget resolution process, its deadlines, composition, and sequencing, can be renegotiated on its own merits instead of under deadline duress.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Introduced repeatedly; not enacted

rows.Additional Tags: personal office, committee, coordination, data transparency
rows.Problem Statement: Casework data is siloed office by office
rows.Problem Description: Every office holds its own casework record, so confirming that a pattern is systemic means calling five or six offices by hand, and no one can see across the institution what constituents are experiencing.
rows.Solution Statement: Shared casework database across both chambers
rows.Solution Description: Build a common casework database with de-identified aggregation across offices, so patterns are visible institution-wide and recurring agency failures surface as data rather than anecdote, with case-level privacy preserved. In the House, the path runs through finishing the personal office rollout of the existing casework document system, extending it to committees whose oversight referral needs differ, and building role-appropriate dashboards: pending-work queues for caseworkers, volume trends for chiefs of staff, and de-identified aggregate patterns that signal systemic agency problems to committee staff.
rows.Horizon Justification: It converts casework from a service each office performs alone into an institutional intelligence source for oversight, a use it cannot serve at all today.
rows.Current Status (Optional): The House has a shared database; the Senate does not; cross-office coordination runs on chat

rows.Additional Tags: personal office, operations, in house development
rows.Problem Statement: Caseworkers are overloaded with routine requests
rows.Problem Description: Much of what arrives is a request for publicly available information, and offices work hundreds of near-identical cases by hand.
rows.Solution Statement: Smart intake forms and AI triage on the front end
rows.Solution Description: Use intake forms that surface referral information and privacy releases at the point of contact, and run document-completeness checks on incoming requests so cases arrive ready to work.
rows.Horizon Justification: It absorbs volume at the door without changing caseworker headcount, the siloed systems, or the agency failures generating the volume, and it risks misclassifying constituents who describe their own situations inaccurately.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #38. The intake and triage system built for one office becomes the working prototype the dedicated casework office's shared assistant replicates chamber-wide, giving that office a maintained, owned version of the same filtering logic instead of a one-off tool.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Individual offices have built versions; no institutional tooling

rows.Additional Tags: CAO, organization, professional development, coordination, personal office
rows.Problem Statement: Casework has no institutional owner
rows.Problem Description: Standards, taxonomy, agency relationships, training, and tooling are handled office by office, shared tools decay unmaintained, and volume keeps rising.
rows.Solution Statement: Dedicated casework office with permanent training and liaison staff
rows.Solution Description: Establish an office owning casework standards, taxonomy, caseworker training, agency liaison, and shared tooling maintenance for both chambers. The House version is a small CAO office as advocate, communication hub, knowledge manager, and data steward for the casework community, building a shared assistant that filters generic requests and checks required documentation before cases reach caseworkers.
rows.Horizon Justification: Congress's highest-volume constituent-facing function gets its first permanent owner, and decaying tools get a maintenance path.
rows.Current Status (Optional): No such office exists; support comes largely from outside. A House version is in POPVOX Foundation FY27 appropriations requests.

rows.Problem Statement: No one owns casework as an institutional function
rows.Problem Description: Caseworker training and peer support are supplied by outside organizations, and the tools caseworkers rely on are built and maintained on grant funding.
rows.Solution Statement: Outside caseworker network and training
rows.Solution Description: Philanthropy-backed training, a peer network, and shared tooling that lift casework practice across many offices at once.
rows.Horizon Justification: It showed what strong casework support looks like and, by supplying it from outside, reduced the pressure on Congress to fund the same capability itself, leaving critical tools dependent on grant cycles.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #38. Outside training and peer networks prove what strong casework support looks like and build the practitioner demand for it; the dedicated casework office then brings that same training and tooling in house, ending its dependence on grant cycles.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Operating today

rows.Additional Tags: procurement, data transparency, personal office, coordination
rows.Problem Statement: Offices' constituent data is held captive by their vendors
rows.Problem Description: Constituent history lives in proprietary vendor systems, so changing tools means losing it, only a handful of vendors are approved, and no office can aggregate across the institution.
rows.Solution Statement: Constituent data layer the institution owns
rows.Solution Description: Separate the data from the application: hold constituent records in a standards-based layer Congress owns, with vendors competing on the functions built above it, and require portability in the next system contract. Conformance to the House-held data layer becomes a condition of vendor approval going forward, which is what makes the standard bind rather than remain optional, alongside an export standard that lets an office change vendors and keep its full history without a migration project. Sequence adoption by demand, starting with offices already planning a change.
rows.Horizon Justification: Ownership of the data changes the market structure permanently, letting offices switch tools without losing history and letting new vendors enter without rebuilding everything.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Next Senate constituent system contract is scheduled for 2028

rows.Problem Statement: Public input arrives at scale but carries no usable signal
rows.Problem Description: Offices cannot process input at volume, most participation diffuses tension rather than informing lawmaking, and nothing tracks whether what a member heard changed what they did.
rows.Solution Statement: Listening at scale with commitment tracking
rows.Solution Description: Run structured deliberation and augmented town halls that convert constituent input into weighted signal about preferences and acceptable tradeoffs, and track public commitments over time against what the member does.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what participation produces rather than adding capacity to process more of the same, and it creates a feedback loop the institution can own.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Tools exist in civic tech; not integrated into congressional workflows

rows.Problem Statement: Offices cannot see who a bill affects at home
rows.Problem Description: Stakeholder contact lives in individual staffers' notes, and connecting a pending bill to the districts, grants, and organizations it touches is manual work that depends on the district team's memory.
rows.Solution Statement: District impact and stakeholder mapping tied to legislation
rows.Solution Description: Link bills and programs to district-level impact data and to a structured record of stakeholder contact, so a member can see who a vote reaches at home and which organizations have weighed in before casting it.
rows.Horizon Justification: It gives offices a durable institutional record where there is only individual memory today, and connects legislating to district outcomes as a standing capability.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Manual today; federal spending data is published but not linked to legislation

rows.Additional Tags: rules, time management, committee, leadership, coordination
rows.Problem Statement: The congressional calendar is set late and does not hold
rows.Problem Description: Committees schedule against each other with no binding deconfliction, the annual calendar changes often, travel days consume a large share of the week, and the Speaker holds unilateral authority to adjourn the House at any time, an ad hoc COVID-era power now written into House rules.
rows.Solution Statement: Stable published calendar with block scheduling and binding deconfliction
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a fixed annual calendar published well in advance, optimized to cut travel days and add session days, with block scheduling of committee meetings and a House rule requiring committees to enter their scheduling data into the Deconflict tool. In practice that means full-week or two-week in-session blocks rather than short legislative weeks, committee days declared off-limits for floor votes during set hours, and three full committee days, which presupposes five-day session weeks, with limited flexibility retained for high-demand committees. Rescind the Speaker's unilateral adjournment authority so session time is set by rule rather than at one member's discretion. The House can do all of this without the Senate.
rows.Horizon Justification: Making the schedule and the power to end it properties of the rules rather than of leadership discretion changes how every member and staffer can plan, and it is one of the few structural changes a single chamber can make alone.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Deconflict tool exists and is voluntary; the Speaker's adjournment authority remains in House rules; recommended by the Bipartisan Policy Center

rows.Additional Tags: time management, committee, coordination, in house development
rows.Problem Statement: The congressional calendar is set late and does not hold
rows.Problem Description: Committee hearings and markups are scheduled without reference to each other, so members with multiple assignments cannot attend either fully. The House Digital Service built a deconfliction tool on a Select Committee recommendation, but its use is voluntary and adoption is low.
rows.Solution Statement: Voluntary committee scheduling deconfliction tool
rows.Solution Description: Provide a shared scheduling tool that surfaces conflicts before hearings are noticed, with recognition or incentives for the committees that use it. Practitioners offer mandating the existing tool explicitly as the more palatable fallback where full block scheduling is unattainable.
rows.Horizon Justification: A voluntary tool depends on the committees that benefit least from coordinating choosing to participate, which is the behavior the problem consists of.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #43. Voluntary use of the Deconflict tool builds the usage data and habit of checking it before scheduling; the House rule making entry mandatory converts that same tool from an optional courtesy into a binding scheduling requirement.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Tool built by the House Digital Service and in use; participation voluntary and low

rows.Problem Statement: Floor access runs entirely through leadership
rows.Problem Description: The consensus and suspension calendars operate at leadership's discretion, so a bill with broad support has no path to the floor independent of leadership's choice. Committees that hold hearings and mark up bipartisan legislation, including routine reauthorizations, have no assurance their work will ever be scheduled, which removes much of the reason to do it.
rows.Solution Statement: Guaranteed regular order and member-driven paths to the floor
rows.Solution Description: Create a guaranteed regular order procedure under which a committee that runs a thorough deliberative process of hearings and markup earns floor consideration for the resulting bipartisan bill, particularly reauthorizations. A bipartisan standard at committee, such as one-third of minority members present and voting, confers priority status or guaranteed consideration within a set number of legislative days, with the Rules Committee still structuring debate but a required vote on the bill as reported rather than on a leadership substitute. Pair this with predictable routes for bills meeting defined thresholds of support, different calendars for different classes of legislation, and bounded layover requirements. The cited precedent is the Texas House local and consent calendars.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes who controls the agenda rather than making leadership's process faster, and it restores the connection between doing committee work and producing law, the incentive that does not exist today.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Recommended by the Bipartisan Policy Center's Working Group on Congress, Courts, and Administrative Law; a workable model is outlined by a Hoover Institution and Sunwater Institute task force

rows.Problem Statement: Amendments have moved off the floor
rows.Problem Description: An open amendment process was normal a decade ago, particularly on appropriations. Structured rules now limit or foreclose amendments, moving negotiation into leadership offices.
rows.Solution Statement: Restore an open amendment process
rows.Solution Description: Return to structured but genuinely open rules on major bills with recorded votes on amendments, so positions are taken on the record and outcomes are decided by votes. The appropriations-specific version requires a recorded vote on every appropriations bill.
