rows.Solution Description: Amend House Rule XV to simplify and update the Calendar Wednesday procedure so committees have a predictable day to bring reported bills directly to the floor, stop the near-weekly unanimous consent dispensing, and require that dispensing carry the consent of a majority of committee chairs. One option requires at least one call per month.
rows.Horizon Justification: It ties floor access to committee action rather than to cosponsorship counts or leadership choice, restoring a route that exists in the rules but is waived away every week.
rows.Current Status (Optional): The rule exists and is dispensed with almost weekly

rows.Problem Statement: Bill text is frozen at introduction
rows.Problem Description: Once introduced, text changes only through committee amendment or reintroduction, so real revision happens in discussion drafts that carry no procedural weight and improvement is deferred to a rushed markup.
rows.Solution Statement: Let sponsors amend introduced legislation before markup
rows.Solution Description: Amend House Rule XII so a primary sponsor may file revised text with the Clerk within a defined window before markup, superseding the introduced version, with versions denoted as H.R. 500(a) and (b), redlines and version history published, and cosponsors notified with a period to withdraw. Modeled on author's amendments in several state legislatures.
rows.Horizon Justification: It makes legislation a versioned document that improves in the open, which changes how bills are developed rather than how they are scheduled.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; standard practice in several states

rows.Problem Statement: A single member can force a vote to remove the Speaker
rows.Problem Description: The motion to vacate is privileged at the instance of one member and lost its committee referral step in 2019, which produced the first successful removal of a Speaker and a persistent instability that shapes every scheduling and negotiating decision.
rows.Solution Statement: Raise the threshold for the motion to vacate
rows.Solution Description: Amend the rules so the motion becomes privileged only above a threshold, such as a majority of the mover's own conference, a fixed number of signatures, or a share of the full House, and restore the requirement that the motion be referred to committee before it ripens. Adopted in the opening-day rules package by simple majority.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes the balance between leadership stability and member leverage, which constrains what any Speaker is able to schedule or negotiate.
rows.Current Status (Optional): The 2019 change removed the referral step; the one-member threshold has been adjusted between Congresses

rows.Problem Statement: No camera-free space exists where members of both parties talk
rows.Problem Description: Cross-party conversation has no informal venue near the floor, so the relationships that make negotiation possible form by accident or not at all.
rows.Solution Statement: Convert the Speaker's Lobby into a bipartisan members-only space
rows.Solution Description: Designate the Speaker's Lobby members-only, excluding press, lobbyists, and non-member staff, and reseat it through the Architect of the Capitol for small-group conversation, making it more attractive than the cloakrooms. The Speaker can act alone; a joint leadership statement makes it durable.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates the chance for relationships without touching the incentives that keep members apart, and the next Speaker can undo it.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #45. Informal cross-party relationships formed in a shared space build the trust members need to reach the bipartisan committee thresholds that a guaranteed regular-order procedure rewards with priority floor consideration.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed previously; the Senate has an equivalent room

rows.Additional Tags: GAO, CBO, CRS, committee, personal office
rows.Problem Statement: Congress underfunds its own capacity
rows.Problem Description: Flat since the early 2000s, the legislative branch budget gives a growing share to the Capitol Visitor Center and Capitol Police as the executive branch it oversees grows enormously.
rows.Solution Statement: Targeted legislative branch capacity initiative
rows.Solution Description: Win a bipartisan leadership commitment to prioritize capacity in the next appropriations cycle, increases targeted to GAO, CBO, CRS, Legislative Counsel, committee funds, and member allowances for staff pay and casework technology, not across the board and excluding security.
rows.Horizon Justification: A single-cycle increase rebuilds capability while the budget's trajectory and the politics behind it stay put; the case recurs annually.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #118. Winning one bipartisan appropriations cycle proves capacity funding can succeed politically, and that coalition is what a formula tying legislative branch funding to a fixed share of spending needs to lock in permanently.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed for the next cycle

rows.Problem Statement: Congress's budget does not scale with what it oversees
rows.Problem Description: The legislative branch has averaged around 0.15 percent of federal budget authority since 1976 and can be quietly starved relative to the government it appropriates for, since its own funding competes annually against every other priority.
rows.Solution Statement: Tie legislative branch funding to a fixed share of federal spending
rows.Solution Description: Establish by standalone legislation, or by a chamber rule setting a target sub-allocation, a floor for legislative branch appropriations as a fixed percentage of non-defense discretionary spending, indexed to a multi-year average and reviewed periodically. A related version funds oversight as a line item set as a percentage of the executive branch budgets being overseen.
rows.Horizon Justification: It removes Congress's capacity from the annual political decision that has eroded it, making the institution's own resourcing structural rather than discretionary.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed independently by multiple groups
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
Recoding America ModSub Submissions (2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Security spending masks the decline in congressional capacity
rows.Problem Description: Growth in Capitol Police, Visitor Center, and Architect of the Capitol funding sits in the same bill as staff, committee, and support agency accounts, so the legislative branch total looks stable while capacity accounts stagnate.
rows.Solution Statement: Separate security funding into its own line
rows.Solution Description: Split security accounts out of the legislative branch capacity accounts, either as distinct lines within the bill or as a separate measure, so the capacity argument can be made on its own terms and the two are not traded against each other.
rows.Horizon Justification: Reorganizing the presentation clarifies the argument without adding a dollar to either side, and the trade-off it exposes still has to be won.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #118. Splitting security spending into its own line isolates the capacity shortfall on its own terms, supplying the evidence needed to peg legislative branch funding to a fixed share of federal spending rather than negotiate it against security every year.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: No one has mapped how congressional capacity is organized
rows.Problem Description: Staffing structure, distribution of expertise, duplication across offices, and service orientation have never been assessed as a whole, so reform proposals are made without a picture of the current state.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional capacity landscape analysis
rows.Solution Description: Commission a comprehensive assessment by a nonpartisan organization with organizational-assessment expertise, run separately for the House and Senate, producing restructuring options rather than diagnosis alone and running in parallel with the appropriations ask rather than delaying it.
rows.Horizon Justification: An assessment produces options that someone else must choose to act on, and the absence of an owner for those options is itself part of the problem being assessed.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #99. The commissioned landscape analysis supplies the organizational assessment and restructuring options that the Secretary General proposal explicitly builds from, converting a one-time diagnostic into the evidence base for a senior civil servant who owns implementation.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed

rows.Additional Tags: committee, personal office, in house development, professional development
rows.Problem Statement: Committees lack expertise in their own subject matter
rows.Problem Description: Many committees have no professional technical staff in the areas they legislate on, and personal offices have none at all, so the expertise in any given hearing belongs to the witnesses.
rows.Solution Statement: Committee-housed technical experts offered as a shared service
rows.Solution Description: House technical experts at the committee level and make them available as a service to all offices, on a pay scale that permits recruiting from the executive branch and industry.
rows.Horizon Justification: It builds permanent subject matter capacity inside the institution and spreads it beyond the committee that hosts it, rather than borrowing expertise per project.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed

rows.Problem Statement: Bipartisan House-passed bills die without Senate coordination
rows.Problem Description: Legislation that clears one chamber with bipartisan support restarts from zero in the other, and vetted bills start over again each Congress.
rows.Solution Statement: Bicameral coordination of bipartisan bills
rows.Solution Description: Convene a bicameral working group of leadership designees and committee staff to identify ten to twenty bipartisan bills eligible for coordination and flag them for prioritized consideration in the other chamber. Pair it with a House fast-track review process letting committees readvance bipartisan bills passed in a prior Congress.
rows.Horizon Justification: A coordination group depends entirely on leadership goodwill in both chambers and covers a handful of bills, leaving the underlying absence of any cross-chamber pathway intact.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #123. The ad hoc working group's practice of identifying and prioritizing bipartisan bills for cross-chamber action builds a working pipeline that a revitalized, rules-based conference process can resolve routinely, replacing leadership goodwill with standing procedure and trained staff.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed

rows.Problem Statement: Almost no one knows how to run a conference committee
rows.Problem Description: The conference process has atrophied: rules are out of date and inconsistent between chambers, and few staff in either chamber have ever convened or run one, so differences get resolved in leadership negotiations instead.
rows.Solution Statement: Revitalize the conference committee process
rows.Solution Description: Review and amend conference rules in each chamber to standardize how conferences are convened, conferees appointed, and reports produced; train dedicated conference clerks in each chamber to hold the institutional knowledge; and build the committee infrastructure to make the process operable. Advanced through each chamber's rules package or a resolution directing the Clerk to publish standard procedures.
rows.Horizon Justification: Restoring a working conference process changes where bicameral differences are resolved, moving them from leadership offices back to the committees that wrote the bills.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Atrophied; conferences are now rare

rows.Problem Statement: The debt ceiling creates a recurring crisis with no fiscal function
rows.Problem Description: The limit does not control spending already enacted, and each standoff threatens borrowing costs and economic stability while consuming the calendar.
rows.Solution Statement: Eliminate the debt ceiling
rows.Solution Description: Abolish the statutory limit and make debt authority automatic upon enactment of the appropriations and authorizations that create the obligations.
rows.Horizon Justification: Removing the mechanism removes the crisis rather than managing it, and it separates the question of how much to spend from the question of whether to pay for what is already spent.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Raised by five trillion dollars in 2025 inside a reconciliation bill; contested
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: The budget resolution process no longer functions
rows.Problem Description: Thirteen of fifty fiscal years since 1976 had no budget resolution, all since 1999; the April deadline has been met four times since 1986; the process waits on a late presidential submission.
rows.Solution Statement: Redesign the budget resolution process
rows.Solution Description: Combine proposed elements: biennial resolution with annual appropriations; May 1 completion in odd years; annual rather than optional reconciliation; no required start from the President's budget; separate budgets and rules for capital, mandatory, and discretionary spending; appropriations and revenue committee leaders on the budget committees; calendar-year fiscal year.
rows.Horizon Justification: It rebuilds the decision structure rather than the deadline; composition and sequencing decide who is in the room when the numbers are set.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Elements advanced by the 2018 Joint Select Committee, which deadlocked
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Fiscal decisions have no enforceable target
rows.Problem Description: Statutory caps have lapsed, statutory pay-as-you-go has never triggered, and the annual process reaches neither revenue nor the tax expenditures that projections put in the trillions.
rows.Solution Statement: Statutory fiscal targets with enforcement triggers
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a multiyear plan built on targets, triggers, and transparency: annual debt or debt-to-GDP targets enforced through a special reconciliation process, a trigger split between spending reductions and revenue increases reaching the broadest possible base including tax expenditures and mandatory health programs, extended baseline projections out twenty-five to thirty years, and caps with statutory enforcement.
rows.Horizon Justification: Binding targets change what the process must produce rather than when it must produce it, which is the difference between a schedule and a constraint.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Multiple competing versions in circulation; the underlying proposals contradict each other on scope
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Programs are funded indefinitely without review
rows.Problem Description: Obsolete and overlapping programs persist because nothing forces a periodic justification, and expired authorizations continue to receive appropriations by default.
rows.Solution Statement: Zero-based budgeting on a rotating cycle with a sunset commission
rows.Solution Description: Require every program to be justified from zero on a ten-year rotation, with a standing sunset commission recommending eliminations and consolidations and a defined path for its recommendations to receive a vote.
rows.Horizon Justification: It makes review a condition of continued funding rather than an optional exercise, which is the mechanism missing behind unauthorized appropriations.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; versions exist at the state level
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Delegated war and emergency powers never return to Congress
rows.Problem Description: Authorities delegated for specific circumstances persist for decades, and emergency declarations are used to justify action that Congress never affirmatively approved.
rows.Solution Statement: Periodic reauthorization of war and emergency powers
rows.Solution Description: Revise the war powers and emergency powers statutes to require affirmative congressional ratification of declarations and force authorizations, with fast-tracked up-or-down votes to reauthorize on a regular cycle, so lapsed authority expires by default rather than persisting.
rows.Horizon Justification: It reverses the default: authority returns to Congress unless renewed, which changes the structural direction of delegation rather than contesting individual uses of it.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed in multiple forms
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congress has delegated major questions and waits for courts to settle them
rows.Problem Description: Significant policy is made through agency rulemaking that Congress never votes on, and the resulting disputes are resolved in litigation years later.
rows.Solution Statement: Fast-tracked votes on major regulations
rows.Solution Description: Require periodic fast-tracked up-or-down votes to enact proposed major regulations and major changes to them, so the significant choices agencies make return to Congress on a defined schedule.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes where major policy decisions are made, and it forces Congress to legislate on questions it currently leaves to agencies and courts.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; related to post-Chevron proposals
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Additional Tags: GAO, CBO, organization, in house development
rows.Problem Statement: Congress cannot independently assess regulations
rows.Problem Description: Agencies produce and analyze their own rules, and Congress has no analytic body of its own to assess proposed or existing regulations, so the record it reviews is the one the regulator wrote.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional Regulation Office
rows.Solution Description: Create a nonpartisan regulation office serving both chambers to analyze proposed and existing rules, paired with increased GAO and CBO funding, alongside a trends-focused technology assessment function.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates analytic capacity Congress owns on the questions where the executive currently holds the entire record, which is the precondition for regulatory oversight after Chevron.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by several groups
rows.Sources:
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Inspectors general answer to the agencies they investigate
rows.Problem Description: IGs are nominally independent yet depend on the agencies they audit for appointment or daily accountability, a vulnerability politically motivated removals exploit, and their findings never structurally feed congressional work.
rows.Solution Statement: Realign inspectors general toward Congress
rows.Solution Description: Shift IG reporting from agency heads to the Comptroller General, or make IGs congressional employees, operational independence intact. Removal only for cause, with written notice to Congress and appeal rights; budget requests sent directly to Congress unmodified, with a funding floor; a quarterly IG and GAO council feeding oversight.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes who the executive branch's internal auditors answer to, the root of every removal fight and of findings that never reach Congress.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed in two forms with different destinations
rows.Sources:
Functional Fusion (April 2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Leadership overrides appropriators unilaterally
rows.Problem Description: Subcommittee chairs no longer hold the influence the position once carried; leadership can override a committee recommendation without a vote, so the committee's work is provisional until leadership agrees with it.
rows.Solution Statement: Require a House vote to override an appropriations recommendation
rows.Solution Description: Change the rules so overriding an Appropriations Committee recommendation requires a vote of the House rather than a leadership decision.
rows.Horizon Justification: It moves a decision from one office to the chamber, restoring the committee's product as the default rather than an opening offer.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by staff and outside experts
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Members cannot object to unauthorized spending
rows.Problem Description: More than thirteen hundred authorizations had expired before FY2025, with hundreds of billions in appropriations tied to them, and no individual member has a procedural way to force the question.
rows.Solution Statement: Member challenge right against unauthorized appropriations
rows.Solution Description: Give each member one challenge per session against any unfunded mandate or unauthorized appropriation, requiring a House vote to override the objection, with an additional challenge earned if the objection is upheld.

rows.Problem Statement: Voters have no clear signal on fiscal accountability
rows.Problem Description: Fiscal arguments run on assertion, and constituents have no straightforward account of what the Congress they are about to vote on did to the deficit.
rows.Solution Statement: Pre-election CBO letter to taxpayers
rows.Solution Description: Require CBO to send taxpayers a plain-language letter before each congressional election stating the deficit and the current Congress's effect on it.
rows.Horizon Justification: It is a disclosure that changes no decision rights and depends entirely on voters acting on information they have largely had access to already.

None of the candidates is a genuine successor; what is needed is an H2+ that embeds fiscal disclosure into a standing, institution-owned accountability mechanism, such as a statutory scorecard tying committee action to deficit outcomes, rather than a one-time pre-election letter.

rows.Problem Statement: Congress and agencies set priorities in parallel and never reconcile them
rows.Problem Description: Agencies produce strategic and performance plans under existing law without any structured congressional engagement, so the branch that writes the mandate never states which priorities it endorses.
rows.Solution Statement: Joint agency performance plan review
rows.Solution Description: Require each agency to submit its annual performance plan to committees of jurisdiction for a structured review of at least sixty days before finalization. Committees issue a formal statement recording priorities endorsed, priorities requested but not adopted, and points of disagreement, and agencies must respond in writing explaining how that input was or was not incorporated.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a recurring, documented moment where the two branches state priorities to each other, which is the loop that currently does not exist at any point in the cycle.

rows.Problem Statement: Diagnosis happens inside the executive branch and arrives filtered
rows.Problem Description: Agencies analyze what is going wrong in a program, political messaging shapes that analysis before it reaches the Hill, and it lands with committee staff who have no structured forum to engage it.
rows.Solution Statement: Cross-branch diagnostic working groups
rows.Solution Description: Give committees standing authority to convene working groups on high-priority issues, jointly staffed by committee staff, career agency staff, and GAO, co-chaired by a member and a senior agency official, with required bipartisan staff participation. Each group publishes interim updates and a final joint report of findings, implementation barriers, and policy options. The chair holds an independent right to release findings, so neither branch can suppress them.
rows.Horizon Justification: It puts congressional and agency staff in a shared analytic process with a protected right of publication, changing where diagnosis is done rather than how it is received.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Minor statutory fixes wait years for a vehicle
rows.Problem Description: Agencies find technical corrections through implementation: small in substance, large in operation, and never worth floor time on their own.
rows.Solution Statement: Technical corrections fast-track docket
rows.Solution Description: Establish a quarterly docket for agency-submitted statutory clarifications, exceptions, and waivers from implementation. GAO and the Parliamentarian jointly certify each as non-substantive; the subcommittee approves or rejects within a set period; approved items ride one consolidated vehicle with expedited floor procedure and a germaneness bar.
rows.Horizon Justification: It clears technical debt without changing how legislation is developed, and certification holds it to changes that are not policy.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #27. The quarterly technical-corrections docket proves agencies and Congress can process small statutory fixes through a certified pipeline, a workflow a version-controlled US Code with consolidated drafting offices would run continuously rather than reassembling case by case each quarter.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; called the most immediately achievable element of its package

rows.Problem Statement: Congress cannot authorize a test of anything
rows.Problem Description: Waivers and pilot authorities are granted sparingly and inconsistently, so alternatives cannot be tried at small scale with congressional visibility. Policy changes arrive all at once or not at all.
rows.Solution Statement: Subcommittee pilot and demonstration authority
rows.Solution Description: Give each subcommittee an annual authorization to approve a limited number of pilots at agencies in its jurisdiction, each with defined objectives, timeframe, evaluation plan, and supplemental appropriations within set parameters. GAO evaluates each pilot on completion, and the subcommittee makes a public determination to scale, redesign, or discontinue, with written rationale. The authority is structured as a condition on delegated authority rather than a legislative veto.
rows.Horizon Justification: It gives Congress a way to learn from a bounded experiment before legislating at scale, a capability the institution has no mechanism for.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Every resource shift requires a full appropriations cycle
rows.Problem Description: Moving money in response to what implementation reveals means waiting for the next bill, so programs run against last year's assumptions until the calendar allows a correction.
rows.Solution Statement: Delegated reprogramming authority for authorizing subcommittees
rows.Solution Description: Grant subcommittees of jurisdiction a defined reprogramming authority within parameters set by the relevant appropriations subcommittee. Agencies submit written justification, subcommittees act within a defined period with approval deemed on inaction, and all approved reprogrammings are publicly reported. Appropriations subcommittees set annual dollar thresholds and eligibility.
rows.Horizon Justification: It distributes a piece of spending discretion to the committees that hold the subject matter knowledge, changing who can act on implementation information and how fast.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; appropriators would contest it

rows.Problem Statement: Every bill is treated the same regardless of the work behind it
rows.Problem Description: A bill developed through evidence and joint diagnosis has no better path than one introduced for a press release, so nothing in the process rewards doing the work.
rows.Solution Statement: Evidence-grounded legislation pathway
rows.Solution Description: Create a defined pathway for bills developed out of joint diagnostic working groups. Qualifying bills carry a GAO-validated implementation assessment documenting findings, options considered, and the evidence base, and receive a guaranteed markup vote within a defined period plus priority floor scheduling. GAO maintains a public registry, and each member has an annual allocation of supported bills.
rows.Horizon Justification: It attaches procedural advantage to evidence rather than to sponsorship or leadership favor, which changes what members are rewarded for doing.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; explicitly creates two tiers of legislation

rows.Problem Statement: GAO serves two branches and arrives after the fact
rows.Problem Description: GAO operates as a retrospective auditor at the end of the process, houses functions that belong to the executive branch, and engages with legislation only once problems are embedded in law.
rows.Solution Statement: Realign and expand GAO as an institution of Congress
rows.Solution Description: Amend GAO's organic statute to establish it as an institution of Congress serving the legislative branch exclusively, transferring executive functions to the relevant agencies. Expand its mission to cover cross-branch facilitation, early-stage policy analysis, and statutory interpretation support, with organizationally distinct units and a structural firewall between audit and advisory work, producing implementation assessments of major legislation under consideration at committee request.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what GAO is for and when it engages, converting the branch's largest analytic asset from an after-action reviewer into a design capability.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Almost all congressional staff are partisan appointees
rows.Problem Description: Nearly all of roughly thirty thousand staff serve at a member's pleasure, fitting for representation but leaving policy analysis, drafting, and implementation assessment without continuity across elections or a shared factual base.
rows.Solution Statement: Nonpartisan congressional staff corps
rows.Solution Description: Create within GAO a corps of roughly three thousand career civil servants, reclassified from existing positions, supporting committees in policy analysis, drafting, working group staffing, and implementation assessment. They hold civil service protections; the Comptroller General appoints them in consultation with committee leadership; partisan activity is barred on duty.
rows.Horizon Justification: A permanent professional layer survives elections, something every comparable institution has and Congress lacks.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; the largest staffing proposal in this set

rows.Problem Statement: Agency knowledge reaches the Hill only through filtered channels
rows.Problem Description: Committees learn what agencies know through testimony, written responses, and technical assistance requests, all delayed and shaped politically, so the operational detail that would inform legislating never arrives in usable form.
rows.Solution Statement: Agency liaison offices inside the Capitol complex
rows.Solution Description: Require each agency above a defined budget threshold to maintain a physical liaison office in the Capitol complex, staffed by career civil servants with operational program expertise and subject to a minimum tenure requirement, supplying timely operational information to staff on request and supporting committee engagement across the cycle.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a permanent, career-staffed channel between the branches that does not run through political appointees, changing what information is available and how quickly.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: Drafting does not account for how a statute will be implemented or read
rows.Problem Description: After Loper Bright, imprecise statutory language produces litigation and instability rather than executive latitude, and Congress has no in-house expertise on how to structure delegated authority that survives constitutional constraints.
rows.Solution Statement: Modernize Legislative Counsel for post-Chevron drafting
rows.Solution Description: Direct House and Senate Legislative Counsel, coordinating with GAO, to expand drafting assistance to reflect operational feasibility and to build expertise in administrative law and program implementation. They would advise members on lawfully structuring conditions on delegated authority, pilot authorizations, and reprogramming, produce interpretation guidance on committee request, and report annually on interpretive questions that warrant legislation.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what drafting expertise covers at the moment statutes are written, which determines how much interpretive room courts and agencies have later.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced

rows.Problem Statement: The executive workforce answers to the President rather than to statute
rows.Problem Description: Political appointees have grown from roughly a thousand in the early 1960s to about four thousand today, thickening a layer that makes agencies more responsive to presidential direction than to faithful execution of legislative mandates.
rows.Solution Statement: Reduce the number of political appointees
rows.Solution Description: Direct a review of all political appointee positions within a year of enactment, identifying those convertible to career status, and set a government-wide reduction target returning toward pre-Watergate levels, to be achieved over four years.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes who executes the laws Congress writes, which conditions whether any oversight or implementation reform reaches the people doing the work.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; contested across administrations

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional productivity is measured by counting bills
rows.Problem Description: Bill counts ignore the tendency to bundle many items into single large measures and treat a landmark statute and a post office naming as equivalent, so the institution is assessed on a number that describes almost nothing.
rows.Solution Statement: Measure output by significant policy change rather than bill count
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a measure of productivity based on laws that alter existing government policy to a significant degree, applied consistently over time, in place of counts of public laws enacted.
rows.Horizon Justification: A better metric changes how the institution is described without changing anything it does, and metrics become distorting as soon as anyone optimizes for them.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #140. Adopting a measure that separates substantive policy change from bill-count padding supplies the definition and evidentiary standard an evidence-grounded pathway needs to certify which bills qualify for guaranteed markup and priority floor scheduling.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Long-standing academic proposal
rows.Sources: Vox, Congressional Dysfunction (Ezra Klein, citing David Mayhew)

rows.Problem Statement: Large technology projects are funded on schedule rather than results
rows.Problem Description: Large House technology projects are funded through multiyear waterfall models, with no way to adjust or discontinue a project based on what it has produced.
rows.Solution Statement: Milestone-based technology funding
rows.Solution Description: Disburse the Modernization Initiatives Fund in tranches released against demonstrated working functionality rather than elapsed schedule, with a user-testing gate before each subsequent tranche. Give the fund explicit discontinuation authority that treats early termination of a failing project as a successful process outcome, cap the initial tranche to force decomposition, and report to House Administration on adjusted and discontinued projects alongside completed ones.

rows.Problem Statement: No one knows which CAO unit owns which service
rows.Problem Description: Offices, vendors, and outside stakeholders cannot tell which unit to approach for which service, so requests route through personal networks.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish a CAO organizational chart
rows.Solution Description: Publish a chart covering each unit, its functional responsibilities, and a designated point of contact. Congressional pay is set office by office with no underlying structure

Each office sets salaries from its own allowance, so pay for the same job varies widely, there is no automatic adjustment for inflation, and a raise depends on a staffer's chief of staff rather than on a schedule. Junior salaries lose to agencies and firms, and mid-career staff leave before their expertise matures.
Put congressional staff on a structured pay scale

Move staff onto a GS-style scale with defined bands by role and seniority and automatic cost-of-living adjustments, raising junior salaries meaningfully while leaving offices discretion within each band, so pay becomes a property of the job rather than a negotiation each staffer runs alone. Proposals converge on the scale but differ on mechanism: apply the GS scale to committee staff or to all staff; make the existing link between the House staff pay cap and Executive Schedule Level II automatic rather than requiring a fresh Speaker's Pay Order each Congress; raise or remove the personal office staff cap, unchanged since the late 1970s while average district population rose from 519,235 to 761,169; and direct the CAO to build an inflation-indexing mechanism applied annually to the office allowance formula.
Automatic adjustment removes the annual political decision that keeps pay flat, so the fix persists through changes in leadership and budget climate rather than eroding between one-time increases.
